title: 🎙️ Repair Culture & Practical Tech
description: Today is about things you can fix, keep running, and pass on — repair culture, right-to-repair wins and setbacks, gear that outlives its manufacturer's support window, and the maker ethos of building to last rather than building to replace. We're interested in tools, devices, and projects where longevity, repairability, and self-sufficiency intersect, especially in rural and off-grid contexts where you can't just run to a repair shop. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Repair Culture & Practical Tech' — the right to repair movement, gear that outlasts its manufacturer, DIY fixes, and tools built for longevity.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical conflict; natural disasters without an engineering or preparedness angle; wildlife and conservation; working-lands policy; Indigenous governance; science discoveries with no DIY or hardware relevance; financial market news.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Hands-on hardware journalism counts fully even without an explicit right-to-repair hook.
- 80-100: Directly about repairability — right-to-repair legislation wins and losses, iFixit-style teardowns scoring repairability, gear designed for user serviceability, products outliving manufacturer support and how owners keep them running, permacomputing, vintage hardware still in active use, open-source hardware, Rossmann-style repair advocacy, 3D-printed replacement parts, battery replacement guides, rural and off-grid repair self-sufficiency.
- 55-79: Hands-on maker and DIY content — builds, modifications, hardware hacks, workshop projects, practical electronics guides with real technical depth, 3D printing hardware and filament, off-grid and solar gear, home lab hardware, tools and workshop equipment, battery and power tech. Most genuine hands-on hardware journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Gadget and device reviews with some technical substance; consumer electronics touching software longevity or ecosystem lock-in; hardware whose selling point is open firmware or modular design.
- 10-29: Surface-level product announcements, gadget speculation, leaked specs, general tech news with no hardware or repair angle.

ANCHORS: 'Framework Laptop 16 teardown: a 9/10 repairability score' → 98. 'Oregon's right-to-repair law takes effect' → 92. 'Building a solar-powered Raspberry Pi weather station' → 68. 'Samsung teases thinner bezels on next Galaxy' → 15.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Fast Company] Can Apple keep its AirPods from becoming ‘PervertPods’?
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Apple’s AirPods are arguably the most iconic headphones ever. The small, glossy, stylish buds are lauded for both their sound and design and are worn by hundreds of millions of people across the globe. 

But come next year, those hundreds of millions of AirPods owners might face a problem they never envisioned: being labeled as creeps or perverts—all for innocuously wearing one of the most instantly recognizable tech gadgets ever made.

That’s because Apple will reportedly release a new AirPods model in 2027 with built-in cameras. Doing so poses an existential threat to the brand reputation of Apple’s most successful product since the iPhone.

From ‘glasshole’ accessory to ‘pervert glasses’

If there’s one thing that can be said about wearables with built-in cameras, it’s that the public has a deep mistrust of the people wearing them. This is because, historically, many camera-enabled wearables have done a poor job communicating to bystanders when the wearer is recording them. It doesn’t help that wearers can often disable or obscure the public-facing alerts manufacturers build into these devices that let others know they may be being recorded.

This uncertainty has caused many people, unjustly or not, to assume the person wearing the wearable is a creep or pervert, and indeed, entire terms have arisen to pejoratively describe such wearers. 

In the early 2010s, people quickly labeled Google Glass wearers “glassholes.” In the 2020s, anyone wearing Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses is often deemed to be wearing “pervert glasses.” When it came to Google Glass, the glasshole blowback got so bad that Google posted a reminder to Glass wearers not to be creepy. 

“[Don’t ]Be creepy or rude (aka, a ‘Glasshole’),” the company wrote in a tip sheet to its users in 2014. “Respect others and if they have questions about Glass don’t get snappy. Be polite and explain what Glass does and remember, a quick demo can go a long way. In places where cell phone cameras aren’t allowed, the same rules will apply to Glass. If you’re asked to turn your phone off, turn Glass off as well.”

But while a “glasshole” implies you were merely being a disrespectful jerk, the “pervert glasses” label applied to Meta’s smart glasses implies something much worse. And indeed, there is no shortage of reports that some wearers of Meta’s smart glasses are using them in privacy-invasive, nonconsensual ways.

Now, concerns about the misuse of so-called “pervert glasses” have become so widespread that there are calls in multiple countries to introduce legislation banning or limiting their use. Meta is preemptively even working on a “kill switch” feature to disable the camera capabilities of its glasses, and has already updated its software to automatically stop recording if someone covers the recording warning light on the frames.

Meta’s moves to reassure the public and governments may be too little, too late, however. The device’s reputation may already be tarnished beyond repair. Indeed, some of Meta’s own smart glasses customers already seem to think so. Owners are reportedly leaving them at home to avoid public shame and being labeled as perverts.

And that’s a problem for Apple’s AirPods—and every person who wears them.

Are all AirPods about to be labeled ‘PervertPods’?

For years now, reports have suggested Apple was working on AirPods with built-in cameras. In August, MacRumors published a video made by Apple confirming such a device is in the works. In the video, a man wearing the camera-equipped AirPods asks the devices to identify and remember the name of a book he is holding.

Bloomberg says these AirPods are on track for a 2027 release. But once they go on sale, if the public blowback against Meta’s “pervert glasses” is anything to go by, owners of even existing AirPods are potentially set to become social pariahs overnight.

This is because, unlike Meta’s smart glasses, which are obviously bulkier than the “dumb” frames people have worn for centuries, the camera-equipped AirPods shown off in Apple’s video look nearly identical to today’s AirPods: small, shiny white buds. That means any public backlash against the camera-equipped AirPods is likely to hit all AirPods users. The AirPods are already so small; who can really tell which model you are wearing?

Once camera-equipped AirPods go on sale, it’s reasonable to assume that, because they look indistinguishable from other models, bystanders will not be able to tell whether someone is wearing the camera models or the regular ones. As a result, they may become suspicious of all AirPods users.

Suddenly, someone wearing AirPods Pro 2 (from 2023) or AirPods 4 (from 2024) may get distrustful or even contemptuous looks from bystanders. In other words, the inevitable “PervertPods” label wouldn’t be limited to camera-equipped 2027 models and above. Such a label would tarnish the entire AirPods brand and make people cautious of users no matter which model they use.

Can Apple prevent AirPods backlash?

So, how can Apple stop this brand destruction?

It doesn’t have many good options. Perhaps the most practical one would be to make the camera-equipped AirPods visually distinguishable at a glance from non-camera-equipped AirPods. Apple could do this by making the camera-equipped AirPods a different color, like midnight blue or cosmic orange. 

However, it’s unlikely that Apple would be willing to ditch the AirPods’ now-iconic shiny white color scheme.

Short of this, Apple will probably rely on changing public perception: educating the public that its camera-equipped AirPods can’t save video and are used only to recognize objects (if that’s what the devices will indeed do). 

But this may not be enough. Apple gave its new Apple Watches, introduced last month, the ability to always record surrounding conversations. The company highlighted that these recordings were never accessible to Apple or the users, and once they had been processed by Siri AI, they would be deleted. Yet despite Apple designing the feature to be privacy-preserving, even the company’s own fan base has expressed serious reservations about it. 

This leads me to believe that, for the brand’s sake, Apple should consider scrapping the camera-equipped AirPods for now. The general public, once eager to embrace every new gadget Big Tech released, is increasingly wary of wearables becoming surveillance tools or enabling nefarious individuals to secretly monitor them. 

Given that this distrust will likely not abate anytime soon, Apple’s wisest move may be to set aside its visual ambitions for the device in favor of focusing on improving what the AirPods already do best: delivering world-class sound quality into our ears.

items.title: [Macworld] Apple tightens macOS Full Disk Access controls as AI agents proliferate
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Macworld

If you’ve been using third-party apps on your Mac, you are probably familiar with a permission dialog box called “Full Disk Access.” It’s sort of a big catch-all permission that lets an application read or write almost any data to your Mac’s drive.

It was originally conceived as a way for apps to be able to fully back up and restore your hard drive, but developers have since used it as a shortcut for auto-updating apps, managment apps, among others. On my Mac, the Adobe Creative Cloud updater wants this permission, as does the Logitech software for managing my keyboard and mouse, and Microsoft OneDrive.

AI agents on the Mac also typically ask for this permission, and it allows them to access information that you may not iwant them to have. If you know where the data is stored, you can access full messages, contacts, photos, emails, browsing history, and much more with just this one setting.

In a note on its Developer Site, Apple says it’s about to crack down on this Full Disk Access abuse by introducing additional controls:

We give developers powerful APIs to build incredible capabilities into their apps for Apple products, backed by a set of controls designed to protect users’ private data. Full Disk Access largely sidesteps these controls in order to allow backup apps to function properly on the Mac. Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users’ full knowledge and understanding. For communication apps, this can also compromise the privacy of the people users are communicating with.

Going forward, we will introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action. Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.

Apple has not yet said what form these controls will take, but it’s likely that it’ll start with sterner wording for this setting, making it clear that any app that requests this access can essentialy see everything on your drive, including every cache and buffer storing info from online services.

We’re starting to hear plenty of horror stories about AI agents having knowledge they’re not supposed to have or wreaking havoc by deleting or modifying important files, and they almost always stem from this simple and over-permissive setting granting access to read and write almost every file on your Mac.

Apple has not given a time frame for this Full Disk Access abuse crackdown, but given how many applications (not just AI agents) use it when they don’t really need to access your entire Mac disk, it can’t come soon enough.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Hubble Space Telescope may have found a planet born after its star died
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

A strange chemical signature in old Hubble observations may point to a planet that formed after its star had already died. Astronomers found unusually high levels of niobium around the white dwarf HS 0209+0832, suggesting some of the star’s expelled material may have assembled into a new gas giant. TESS data also hints at a Jupiter-sized planet orbiting just 3.7 million miles from the star.

From "urban mining" to life cycle assessments (LCAs), professionals, organizations, and researchers are exploring different solutions and strategies to address the same overarching challenge. Project (Un)Build is a research initiative developing reversible timber construction methods that use straps and friction pads to facilitate material reuse. It contributes to the ongoing debate and reflection on the act of building itself.

items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

A Senate investigation on AI data centers question that costs and benefits that AI hyperscalers show when they apply for permits to put up their developments. The report says that these claims are misleading and that they don't show the real impact of these sites on the local economy.
